Messages.Author: David Pontes
Messages.Body:
On 13 Oct 1996, Gomi no Sensei wrote:

> In article <53ouq1$6...@nntp-3.io.com>, Chris Gottbrath <cl...@io.com> wrote:
> > Silly Question:
>
> > Is there any reason that one could not play a unique card that had
> >been burned for whatever reason? For example if I play Renegade Garu, it
> >gets burned in combat and I have another in my deck that I wish to recruit
> >later on in the same game.

> > If the answer is no then does the same go for named cards?
> >(Thaddius Zoe or Mr. Winthrop)
>
> Yep. You can replace burned uniques all day long.
>

According to the official rules, yes. But I'm compiling a set of
guidelines that prevent this absurdity. They are broad guidelines, but you can
solve most problems with a reality check. The main problem is that you
should play the RPG in order to make these reality ckecks more accurate:

- These rules apply to unique locations, retainers, minions (every
named vampire is unique) and equipment. "Unique Master"s (Fame,
Bureaucratic Overload, et al) are not included.

- There's a difference between "discard" and "burned": discard
happens when it doesn't matter what the card says. Burn happens when the
card was destroyed by another's intervention.

- There's another ash pile: the unique pile. There we'll place
all the uniques that are burned (by the latter definitions).

- A card that's in the unique pile can never be brought into
play.

- The ash pile and the unique pile work as if they are the same.
Any activity that would target the ash pile can reach any one of these
piles.

Quite simple! This will surely make the game much more realistic.
I'd be more than happy to hear from you what you think about it. :)

David Pontes

Messages.Author: theCorrupter
Messages.Body:
On 18 Oct 1996, L. Scott Johnson wrote:

> rob...@adam.com.au (robert donoghue) writes:

[Re: Changing rules on unique cards]

> >Much simpler way: the one per deck rule. One of each unique (vamp,
> >location, etc.), no more allowed in your library/crypt.

> This solution, while simpler, is not sufficient. It still allows for
> each Methuselah to have a Nik is her crypt, for example, and to bring
> one out after someone else's has been burned.

To add to this, not only does it not stop multiple Niks, it really isn't
good for the game. By only allowing one for each unique, whether or not
the narrative improves, the game becomes more based on luck rather than on
deck design skill.

Another drawback (though only a temporary one) is that clans from Dark
Sovereigns and Ancient Hearts will have a hard time making a decent crypt.

The original solution (to not allow the _return_ of burned uniques) is
better in that deck construction is not hurt. However, I'm not convinced
the additional comlexity is necessary.

Alright, how about this:
you take a pack of ordinary playing cards. Each player sheffles them in
turn. They are cut. The 1st player takes a card from the top, notes the
value (i.e 2 is bad, ace is very good), replaces it. TYhey are shuffled.
The next player cuts, draws a card, etc. They go in order of card value,
each declaring one unique crypt and one unique library card. Once a card
is declared, you cannot then name it. This continues until no-one wishes
to or is able to name a unique card.
They put their cards into their deck, shuffle, play.

Messages.Author: theCorrupter
Messages.Body:
On 21 Oct 1996, robert donoghue wrote:

> James Puzzo (jam...@dgii.com) wrote:

> : The arson of a building, however, I would explain as you making the
> : investment to rebuild it, thus bringing it under your control.

> Then why does building an art gallery cost less than buying an assault
> rifle???
> :)

Ah. It's been awhile.

There is a simple reason. Remember that pool is an abstract measure of
your influence, holdings, and basic status with the other Methuselahs.
From a game world standpoint, there are far more Methuselahs than the 2 to
7 others sitting at your table. Thus, their opinions of you are quite
influential on your ability to do things. Secondly, these Methuselahs are
near omniscient. If you influence one of your minions into getting an
assault rifle, They will know. Using such modern tools as assault rifles
is banal and smacks of lowering oneself to the standards of human (read:
cattle) conflict. Such an action is both foolish seeming, and influence
expensive (getting an illegal weapon into the hands of an undead creature
who might not have records remaining of their mortal existence). The loss
of pool is a loss of support from "other" Methuselahs as well... Art
museums are far less of a lowering of status.



Messages.Author: James Puzzo
Messages.Body:
robert donoghue (rob...@adam.com.au) wrote:
: What? You thought i was serious? Oh dear. :) (that was a joke too...)

I knew you weren't serious. But, regardless, it was a valid description.

: Well, sure, but if you want to say this then "pool" could be absolutely
: anything.

Well, not absolutely ANYTHING.

: It could be the measure of your cheese collection. You could

: offer a piece of edam in exchange for Donald Cruez's alleigance. It could
: be a combination of limitless variables; it cannot be defined.

Well, not defined as a specific commodity. But if you think of pool as the
sum total of the resources which you have available to you to gain and
maintain influence, then you have a handle on it. If you really _want_
to have a specific commodity in mind, that's where those storytelling
variants come in... ;)

: BUT, surely by any means, it MUST be easier, say, to go to some guy

: and purchase an uzi than it is to bribe the boss of an art gallery,

You are correct that it is _probably_ easier to actually purchase an uzi.
But buying an uzi and getting someone to use are two totally different things.
This is where the difference between pool and cash lies.

As I understand it, in the world of vampires, guns are taboo -- so it takes
more influence for you to force a minion to use one that it does to keep
and maintain influence over an art museum... a respected investment. ;)

: and say "hey, toreadors, come over here! it's art! Now, i have a
: favour to ask..."

And again, jokingly or not, it's a valid (if thin) story to describe your
investment in influence.

-spongy

Now you're starting to split hairs. Yes, there are probably many
unscrupulous vampires, but consider that the vampires that participate _in
this game_ aren't as unscrupulous as some. And that the ones that are
more unscrupulous, and thus more likely to use guns, have special abilities
which help lower the cost of equipping with them and using them.

-spongy
